synthetic.name: Feedstock (Natural Gas, Coal, or Hydrogen)
synthetic.notes: Roughly 99% of ammonia synthesis hydrogen is currently fossil-fuel-derived, dominated by natural gas via steam methane reforming, with coal gasification used in some regions, especially China. High transparency: natural gas and coal supply volumes are well tracked by national energy statistics.
synthetic.data_quality: High: national energy statistics and IEA/IFA supply data

synthetic.name: Haber-Bosch Synthesis (Ammonia)
synthetic.notes: D-heavy imbalance. Century-old, capital-intensive, high-pressure and high-temperature process. Energy intensity 7.7-10.1 kWh per kg NH3. Direct emissions approximately 450-500 Mt CO2e per year globally, about 1.3% of global GHG emissions. High transparency at the plant-capacity level (IFA, national industry data) but emissions-intensity reporting per facility is inconsistent.
synthetic.data_quality: High for capacity, Medium for facility-level emissions intensity

synthetic.name: Downstream Conversion (Urea, Ammonium Nitrate, Nitric Acid)
synthetic.notes: Urea, ammonium nitrate, and nitric acid together represent about 91% of nitrogen fertilizer use. This is the stabilization step that converts ammonia into transportable, storable products. High transparency: production volumes tracked by IFA (International Fertilizer Association) and national statistics.
synthetic.data_quality: High: IFA and national production statistics

synthetic.name: Distribution and Storage
synthetic.notes: Global trade and logistics network moving fertilizer from production plants to agricultural regions, including nitrogen-deficient regions that face access and price barriers. Medium-high transparency: trade flows tracked by UN Comtrade and IFA.
synthetic.data_quality: Medium-High: UN Comtrade and IFA trade flow data

synthetic.name: Field Application
synthetic.notes: Secondary bottleneck. C-heavy imbalance: application rates and timing are largely uncontrolled at the farm level in most of the world, with little real-time constraint (D) matching the volume of nitrogen applied (C). Low transparency: farm-level application data is fragmented and rarely centrally reported.
synthetic.data_quality: Low: farm-level application data fragmented, rarely centrally reported

synthetic.name: Environmental Return (N2O Emissions, Runoff, Leaching)
synthetic.notes: Worst phase in the chain. Failure zone (below the 61.8 stability threshold). Extreme C-heavy imbalance: global cropland nitrogen-use efficiency is only about 55% as of 2020 (recovered from a low of approximately 30% in 2000), meaning roughly 45% of applied nitrogen is lost to the environment as ammonia volatilization, nitrate runoff and leaching (causing eutrophication and algal blooms), and nitrous oxide emissions. This is the textbook C-type biogeochemical-flows planetary boundary transgression described in this repo's Paper 19 (docnav/Research/papers/19_ndc-planetary-boundaries-supply-chain.md): uncontrolled output flows exceeding ecological reabsorption capacity, unconstrained by any effective D-side limiting mechanism at the field-to-environment interface. Very low transparency: diffuse, unmonitored, non-point-source pollution by nature.
synthetic.data_quality: Very Low: diffuse, unmonitored, non-point-source pollution

system.interpretation: The ammonia and nitrogen fertilizer chain scores 82.6% average balance (Good zone), but this chain-average figure is deceptively high: it masks a severe tail-end structural failure. Phase 5 (Environmental Return, 57.6%) is the only phase in the chain below the 61.8% stability threshold, a Failure-zone result driven by the collapse of global cropland nitrogen-use efficiency (approximately 55% as of 2020, having fallen to a low of approximately 30% in 2000 from an approximately 80% baseline in 1960). Phase 4 (Field Application, 67.7%) is the secondary bottleneck, Stressed zone, well below the chain average. Both phases share the same C-heavy structural signature: uncontrolled output (nitrogen applied, then lost) exceeding the weak constraint layer (D) that would otherwise bound it. This is a textbook C-type biogeochemical-flows planetary boundary transgression per this repo's Paper 19 (docnav/Research/papers/19_ndc-planetary-boundaries-supply-chain.md), distinct from a D-type constraint failure such as climate or freshwater boundary transgression.

baseline.label: Current state (2020-2026 baseline, single scenario)
baseline.notes: pi = chain average balance (82.6, Coherent zone), deceptively high given the severe Phase 5 tail-end failure. phi = proportional value distribution (58.0, Failure zone): farmers in nitrogen-deficient regions face access and price barriers while other regions over-apply, so value and physical nitrogen are not proportionally distributed to where they generate the most food output per unit of environmental loss. sqrt2 = structural overhead (72.0, Stressed zone): Haber-Bosch plants are necessarily capital-intensive fixed infrastructure, a moderate but largely irreducible structural cost. ln2 = value transformation (65.0, Stressed zone, just above the Failure boundary): global cereal nitrogen-use efficiency fell from approximately 80% in 1960 to approximately 30% in 2000, then partially recovered to approximately 55% by 2020, a value-transformation process that has never returned to its historical efficiency baseline. e = financial abstraction (50.0, Failure zone, the weakest axis): sustainability-linked agricultural finance and carbon markets for nitrous oxide abatement remain nascent and are rarely tied to measurable nitrogen-use-efficiency outcomes at the farm level. ln2 and e are the standout failure signals: a decades-long value-transformation gap (ln2) that has never been closed by financial instruments capable of pricing the externality (e).
